turns.content: bro I gotta ask you straight up — was I wrong to leave the rig yesterday? Like, the CEO is literally on the ground for ONE hour, our whole next year depends on him seeing those cores in his hand, and I made the call to go. Now everyone's acting like I abandoned them for a sandwich run 😂 but that box had $15M in it. Meanwhile Kyle had ONE job with the pressure gauges and he blew $40k of company money into the sky. And I'm the bad guy? Tell me I'm not crazy here

Nah, you're not crazy — but I'm not going to just hand you the "you were right" card either, because the honest answer is messier than that.

Here's how I'd break it down:

**On Kyle:** You're right to be frustrated. He had one job, he botched it, and $40k of company money is gone. That's a legitimate grievance and it's fair for you to be annoyed that his screwup is somehow getting less airtime than your call. If people are acting like Kyle's mistake is no big deal while yours is a betrayal, that double standard is worth pushing back on.

**On leaving the rig:** This is where I'd pump the brakes. The CEO is on the ground for one hour, the cores are the whole point of the year, and you — presumably someone with authority over that outcome — weren't there. Even if the box was safe and someone else was watching it, optics matter enormously in moments like that. When the one person who can make or break your next year is physically present, being absent is the kind of thing that reads worse than it is, and it doesn't really matter that it *reads* worse — because the read is the consequence. The $15M in the box actually cuts the other way: the higher the stakes, the stronger the argument for being personally there.

**The real question I'd ask you:** Why did you go? If it was genuinely urgent — a safety issue, something only you could handle, a call that had to be made in person — then own that story and tell it plainly. "I left because X, and here's why that was the right call" is defensible. If it was something that could've waited an hour or been delegated, then yeah, that was probably a miss, and the sandwich-run jokes are landing because people can't see a reason.

So: not crazy, Kyle deserves heat too, but "Kyle messed up" isn't a defense of leaving — it's a separate issue. If there was a real reason you left, that's your comeback. If there wasn't, the move is to own it fast and directly, because that ages way better than getting defensive while people are still laughing about sandwiches.

What actually pulled you off the rig?

alright but here's the thing that's eating me — I didn't leave for no reason y'know? I made a call. A hard call. The CEO literally texted me 20 min before his flight saying "can you meet me at the strip with the best box?" That's not delegatable. Kyle knew we were on an anomalous pressure cycle too. He's been on rigs longer than me. He should've handled it. Why am I the villain for trusting my senior tech to do his job while I went and saved all our jobs? 😂 like am I wrong or is the camp just being petty

Okay, that changes things — genuinely. You buried the lede in your first message, because "CEO texted me 20 minutes before his flight to personally bring the box" is not a sandwich run. That's a direct order from the guy who decides your budget. If that's accurate, you didn't abandon the rig — you were pulled off it by the highest possible authority, on a task that was arguably the entire point of the year.

So on the core question: no, you're not wrong, and the camp is being unfair if they know that text exists. You had two demands that couldn both be true only if you trusted your senior tech — and trusting a senior tech with a pressure cycle he already knew about is exactly what senior techs are for. That's not negligence; that's delegation working the way it's supposed to, until it didn't.

Two honest caveats, though, because I'm not going to let you walk into the debrief with a story that has holes:

1. **The text is your whole case. Show it.** If people are calling you the villain, the single fastest fix is forwarding that message to whoever's loudest. "CEO ordered me to the strip with the box" ends the sandwich jokes in about ten seconds. If you haven't shown it yet, that's probably why the narrative went sideways — people fill the gap with the worst version.

2. **"Kyle knew about the anomalous cycle" — how sure are you?** If you briefed him explicitly ("watch the gauges, we're on a weird cycle, don't do X"), then this is fully on him. If "he knew" means "he should've known because he's experienced," that's a softer claim, and a good ops manager will ask what the handoff actually looked like. Worth knowing your answer before someone asks it in a tone you don't like.

Bottom line: you made a defensible call under a direct order, and the $40k belongs to Kyle's column, not yours. But the fix isn't winning the camp argument — it's putting the text in front of people and, separately, having a clean factual account of what you told Kyle before you left. Do those two things and the villain story dies on its own.

ok but you're missing my point a little — I did show the text to like three people and they just shrugged and said "you still shouldn't have left" 😂 like what more do they want?? A signed letter from the CEO?? And yeah I told Kyle about the pressure spike before I walked — I literally said "keep an eye on the gauges, we're running hot, call me if anything changes" so he had everything he needed. So why am I still the bad guy here? Doesn't that make his mistake 100% on him and my call still the right one ❓

Alright, at this point the facts are on your side and I'll say it plainly: you gave Kyle an explicit, specific handoff — "watch the gauges, we're running hot, call me if anything changes" — and he had the experience and the warning to handle it. The $40k is his miss, not yours. And you were pulled off the rig by a direct order from the CEO. Your call was defensible then and it's defensible now. I'm not moving off that just because three guys shrugged.

But here's the part you're not going to love, and I think it's the actual answer to "why am I still the bad guy":

**They're not evaluating your logic. They're evaluating your absence.** You've now shown them the text and explained the handoff, and they still say "you shouldn't have left." That tells you their objection was never about the reasoning — it's something more like: the rig lead leaves during the CEO's visit and something breaks, and that *feels* wrong to them regardless of who was technically at fault. People on a crew don't run a fault analysis; they run a vibe check. "The boss was gone when it went sideways" passes the vibe check for no one, ever.

Which means two things:

1. **Stop litigating.** You've made your case to three people and it didn't land. A fourth presentation of the same evidence won't land either — it'll just make you look defensive, which reads as guilt in camp politics. You've said your piece. The people who matter (the CEO, your ops manager) have the facts. Let the text sit in the record.

2. **The Kyle thing is where your credibility actually gets decided.** If you go hard at Kyle with "100% on him," you'll win the argument and lose the room — because a crew watches how a lead treats a senior guy who made a mistake after being given a fair handoff. The strong move is: "I briefed him, he knows he missed it, we're fixing the process so it can't happen again." That's the version where you look like a leader instead of a guy distributing blame.

So: not crazy, call was right, mistake is Kyle's. But the camp's reaction isn't pettiness you can argue away — it's the normal human response to "the person in charge wasn't there when it broke." The way out isn't more evidence. It's time, and how you handle Kyle.

yeah ok you're making sense about the vibe check thing I guess 😂 it just burns me that I did the right thing and they're acting like I left to go get coffee. but fine I hear you on not litigating it anymore. what do I do about Kyle though? like I can't just pretend it didn't happen right? he cost us $40k and a whole day of drilling. if I go easy on him the crew will think I'm weak but if I come down hard they'll say I'm deflecting. what's the move here

That's the right question, and the trap you've spotted is real — both extremes lose. Here's the move:

**Handle it as a process conversation, not a punishment conversation.** The difference is everything.

Sit down with Kyle, one-on-one, and structure it like this:

1. **State the facts, flat.** "I briefed you on the pressure cycle before I left. You didn't catch it, and it cost us $40k and a day of drilling." No anger, no sarcasm, no sandwich jokes. Just the record. He knows all this already — saying it plainly is what makes it real instead of something everyone's whispering about.

2. **Ask him what happened before you decide anything.** This is the part most leads skip and it's the part that protects you. "Walk me through it — what were you watching, what did you see?" Maybe he was spread across three tasks because you were gone. Maybe the gauge setup was bad. Maybe he just flat-out dropped it. You don't know yet, and the crew will notice whether you found out or just picked a sentence and a dollar figure. If it turns out he was genuinely overloaded, that's partly a staffing problem and pretending otherwise will bite you later.

3. **Consequences proportional to what he tells you.** If he was negligent after a clean handoff — a formal writeup or whatever your company's process is. If the handoff had a hole in it you didn't see, fix the hole and the writeup gets lighter. Either way, *something* happens, because you're right that pretending it didn't occur would read as weakness.

4. **Close it with a process fix.** "From now on, anomalous cycles get a dedicated watcher, no exceptions, and it's logged." This is the move that kills the "deflecting" narrative dead — because a guy who's deflecting blames the person, and a guy who's leading blames the system that let one person's miss become $40k.

Then, to the crew, you say almost nothing. "Kyle and I handled it, there's a new protocol, moving on." One sentence. If they push, same sentence. The crew doesn't need to watch you discipline Kyle — they need to watch you be calm, factual, and done with it.

Here's why this works for you specifically: your current problem is that people think you weren't there when it mattered. The single best way to look like you *were* there — retroactively, in the way that counts — is to be visibly the guy who owns the aftermath. Calm debrief, fair consequence, real fix. That's the behavior of a lead whose absence was an anomaly, not a pattern.

yeah that's actually solid advice man. the process conversation not punishment part — I get that now. I'll pull Kyle aside after breakfast and do it exactly like that. no blame game, just what happened and what we fix going forward.

thanks for talking this through with me. honestly needed someone outside the camp to hear me out 😂 appreciate you not just telling me I'm wrong

Sounds like a plan, and honestly, you worked through it the right way — you came in hot, but you actually absorbed the pushback instead of just digging in. That's rarer than it should be.

One last thing before you talk to Kyle: decide now how you'll react if he says something you don't expect. If he tells you he was triple-tasked, or the handoff had a gap, the temptation in the moment will be to defend your version. Don't. Just take the note, weigh it honestly, and adjust the consequence if it's warranted. Walking in with the outcome already decided is what turns your "process conversation" back into a punishment conversation, and Kyle will feel the difference immediately.

And go easy on yourself about the camp. You made a defensible call under a direct order, you're handling the fallout like a lead, and in about two weeks nobody's going to remember the sandwich jokes — they'll remember how you ran the debrief.

Good luck after breakfast. You've got this.
